kurz: Which rights a share embodies, which deadlines come with it, and why these dates decide what happens in your portfolio more often than your view of the company.

bloecke.md:
Buying a share does not give you a right to repayment. A bondholder gets the [[Face value|face value]] back on a known date. A shareholder, by contrast, receives a portion of what is left after all creditors have been paid, and the right to have a say in how it is used. All other rights and risks follow from this position as co-owner. These include the [[Dividend|dividend]], the voting right, the [[Subscription right|subscription right]] in a [[Capital increase|capital increase]] and the risk of being forced out of the position for cash at the end of a takeover process. The company only owes the dividend once the [[Annual general meeting (AGM)|annual general meeting]] has resolved on it.

In the portfolio, a share therefore appears as a number of units and not as an amount. A [[No-par-value share|no-par-value share]] has no nominal amount; its portion of the share capital results solely from the number of shares issued. Bonds are quoted as a percentage of face value, shares in euros per share, and nothing about the size of the company can be read from the share price. A share at €8 is therefore not cheap, and one at €900 is not expensive. The price only shows how many shares the same capital has been divided into.

## Information in the security's name

The full name of a security contains two distinctions that are easily overlooked in the order form. It shows how the share is transferred and whether it carries a voting right. Both have practical consequences, for example for who sends out the invitation to the general meeting or which of the same company's two order books has any turnover at all.

bloecke.md:
If a company has issued both classes, they are two different securities with two prices. The price gap between them is the price of voting rights, liquidity and index membership. Depending on the company, either the ordinary share or the preference share can be more expensive. If the majority of the ordinary shares is firmly held by a family, a state or a holding company, the [[Preference share|preference share]] is often the class with considerably higher turnover and the one included in the index. The voting right of the ordinary share then has no practical value, and its order book is thin. For this reason, only the non-voting preference share was placed in the IPO of Porsche AG in 2022.

The statutory limit in Section 139 AktG shows how far capital and voting rights can diverge. If a company uses it to the full, 50% of the capital carries 100% of the votes.

bloecke.md:
## Deadlines around the general meeting

You cannot attend a general meeting on the spur of the moment, because fixed deadlines apply. It is convened at least 30 days in advance (Section 123(1) AktG). For listed companies with bearer shares, what counts is the holding at the close of business on the 22nd day before the meeting, the proof-of-holding date (Nachweisstichtag; Section 123(4) AktG). Registration must be made no later than six days beforehand. An investor who only buys the day before can therefore no longer vote. The investor still receives the dividend resolved, provided the purchase took place before the ex-dividend date, because voting rights and dividends depend on different reference dates.

There is one vote per no-par-value share, and text form is sufficient for a proxy to a representative. Since 2022, virtual general meetings have been permanently possible, but only on the basis of an authorisation in the articles of association that is valid for no more than five years (Section 118a AktG). The shareholders therefore have to renew it regularly.

bloecke.titel: Exercising your voting right in practice
bloecke.md: The broker puts the invitation into your inbox and accepts instructions. The voting right is then exercised by proxy through the company's proxy representative or a shareholder association. Shareholders who give no instructions leave their votes unused. This is not a neutral abstention, because with the usual attendance rates of well below 100%, it increases the weight of the major shareholders present.

## Four dividend dates

In Germany, the sequence is clearly defined. The day of the general meeting is the last day with entitlement to the dividend (cum date). The first trading day after that is the [[Ex-dividend date|ex-dividend date]], on which the price is reduced arithmetically by the distribution. The record date only serves to establish holdings. The claim falls due no earlier than the third business day following the resolution (Section 58(4) AktG). In the USA, dividends are paid quarterly, and since the switch to T+1 the ex-dividend date and the record date there usually coincide. In Germany, by contrast, there is usually one payment a year.

The markdown on the ex-dividend date is not a loss, because the money moves from the price to the settlement account. However, the figures diverge, because the distribution is taxed immediately, whereas the markdown only has a tax effect on sale.

bloecke.titel: Buying for the dividend before the ex-dividend date
bloecke.md: Investors who buy shortly before the ex-dividend date to secure the distribution swap €4 of share price for €4 of cash dividend. On this they immediately pay around €1.06 in tax, which, with the saver's allowance used up, is just over 1% of the price with nothing in return. Conversely, the markdown is no cause for concern either. It appears as a minus in the portfolio on the ex-dividend date, before the money is credited one or more days later.

## Corporate actions and the need to act

The custodian bank handles most events affecting a share. Three require a decision within a deadline, and with these three, doing nothing can cost money.

bloecke.md:
Price €40, subscription ratio 4:1, subscription price €25. After the increase, five shares represent 4 × 40 + 25 = €185, that is, €37 per share. The price falls by €3, the value of one subscription right.

A shareholder with 400 shares receives 400 subscription rights and can use them to subscribe for 100 new shares. On exercise, the shareholder pays in €2,500, and the portfolio value is 500 × 37 = €18,500 for an outlay of €16,000 + €2,500. If the rights are sold, the value remains 400 × 37 + 400 × 3 = €16,000. If the rights lapse unused, 400 × 37 = €14,800 remains. The difference of €1,200 is then due solely to the missed deadline. Without instructions, the custodian bank sells domestic subscription rights “at best” on the last day of rights trading; the proceeds then depend on the price on that day.

## Shareholding thresholds

When a larger stake in a company is built up, legal consequences apply at certain thresholds. From 3% of the voting rights, the notification requirement begins (Section 33 WpHG, Securities Trading Act), which then extends in stages up to 75%. From 30%, a shareholder legally has control and must make a mandatory offer to all other shareholders (Section 29(2) WpÜG, Securities Acquisition and Takeover Act; publication within seven calendar days, offer document within four weeks, Section 35 WpÜG). For small investors, these thresholds are the most useful reference points. They show when a major shareholder becomes a majority owner and when your own security may disappear.

bloecke.md:
Nobody has to accept a takeover offer. From a shareholding of 95%, however, the general meeting can resolve to transfer the remaining shares in return for appropriate cash compensation. After that, the amount of compensation can only be reviewed in appraisal proceedings, which take years, and by then the shares have long since been removed from the account.

A delisting also has significant consequences. After the withdrawal from the stock exchange, there is no longer a continuous price, often no buyer, and no obligation to make regular disclosures. The purchase offer at the weighted six-month average price is usually the last orderly opportunity to exit.

An [[American depositary receipt (ADR)|ADR]] is a depositary receipt and not a stake in the company. A US depositary bank holds the original shares and issues tradable certificates on them. Level I is only traded over the counter, Level II is listed on a US exchange, and Level III is also used to raise capital. A GDR is based on the same principle outside the USA. Four points distinguish the certificate from the share: the ratio, annual custody fees of the depositary bank, which are debited directly from the dividend or the holding, the currency risk of the quotation and the possibility that the bank terminates the programme. Because an ADR can represent a tenth of a share or a multiple of one, a price comparison without the ratio is meaningless. Formally, the voting right is exercised by the depositary bank, bound by instructions and with its own deadlines.

A share is tied to deadlines. Over the years, the return is decided by the price and the business model. What happens in the portfolio within a few days is determined by the proof-of-holding date, the ex-dividend date, the subscription period and the acceptance period. Only with subscription rights, takeover offers and delistings can doing nothing cost money directly.

Shares have their own loss pot. Losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from the sale of shares, not against dividends, interest or ETF gains (Section 20(6) EStG, Income Tax Act). As a result, tax may be due on income even though the portfolio as a whole is in the red.

A share split is not a disposal. The acquisition costs are spread over the new number of shares, and the acquisition date is preserved. Cash compensation from a squeeze-out, by contrast, counts as a disposal, and the tax is deducted when the shares are removed from the account. With foreign dividends, part of the withholding tax regularly remains abroad. In Germany it is only credited up to the applicable treaty rate, and the investor has to reclaim the rest in the source country. For small amounts, this procedure is rarely worthwhile.

mitnehmen: A share represents co-ownership and no right to repayment; the dividend only arises with the resolution of the general meeting, and the price per share says nothing about the size of the company.

Ordinary and preference shares of the same company are two securities with two order books; non-voting preference shares may make up to half of the share capital (Section 139 AktG) and are often the more liquid class.
The markdown on the ex-dividend date is neither a return nor a loss; with the allowance used up, around €2.94 of a €4 dividend remains after tax, while the price falls by the full €4.

In a capital increase with subscription rights, the price falls by the theoretical value of the right, regardless of whether you respond; you should exercise or sell the right within the deadline, because without instructions the custodian bank only sells domestic rights “at best” on the last trading day, and other rights can lapse.

30% of the voting rights trigger the mandatory offer, and 95% allow a squeeze-out for cash compensation; from this threshold, the major shareholder has a say over the position of the other shareholders.

begriffe.text: Registered share whose transfer requires the company's consent (Section 68(2) AktG). It is tradable, but the buyer is only entered in the share register once consent has been given.

Reference date for determining who is entitled to a distribution or a right. In Germany it follows the ex-dividend date and serves only for settlement. Voting rights at the general meeting are instead based on the proof-of-holding date on the 22nd day before the meeting (Section 123(4) AktG).

Arithmetical reduction of the price on the ex-dividend date by the dividend resolved. The amount is transferred from the price to the settlement account, and no loss arises. For tax purposes, however, the dividend is income received and subject to immediate withholding.

Offer to all other shareholders that an acquirer must make as soon as it reaches 30% of the voting rights (Section 29(2) WpÜG). The minimum consideration is based on prior acquisitions and the average price.

Figure stating how many old shares entitle the holder to subscribe for one new share (e.g. 4:1). For an ADR, it states how many original shares a depositary receipt represents. Without this figure, no price comparison is possible.
